utterances.text: And in your medical opinion, what kinds of things could cause the type of injury that is described here in the Latin, an explosive injury of the manner that you just detailed for us?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Those injures are caused by fragmentation of mines or explosives such as mortar shells or cannon shell and also such injuries may be caused by the explosion of hand-grenades. So hand-grenades may also be the cause of such injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How would a gun-shot wound compared [sic] to the type of wound that is described in this document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: There are differences between blast wounds and gun-shot wounds. Depending on the angle at which the projectile enters the body, it could be round or oval in form. If the projectile has not been damaged before entering the body, the edges of the wound are straight and smooth as opposed to wounds caused by shrapnel, where injuries are irregular forms. So are the edges. They can be of different shapes, another difference is depending on the distance from which projectiles were fired. If it is point blank, a gun-shot injury is probably an entry and exit wound except when it hits a bone such as the hip bones, which are very thick and in which a projectile may get stuck. As opposed to blast wounds where there are numerous channels that destroy much more soft tissue, because the shrapnel has an irregular pattern of penetrating a human body. And as this person was admitted to a hospital when the wounds were dressed, pieces of shrapnel are lodged at smaller depth than gun-shot projectiles. And the persons who dressed the wounds can very easily make a distinction between shrapnel and gun-shot projectiles and the injuries caused by them. In this specific case, taking into account that the person was admitted to a hospital for a period of 26 days, probably it was a mine or an explosive, such as mortar shell or a cannon shell, and that these were serious injuries which are not described in this discharge list, but such injuries required a long period of treatment as verified by the doctors in their finding.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've had discussions with Mr. McCloskey of the Prosecution and I understand there is a CLSS translation of this document that has the Latin translated into -- I can't remember if it's English because I only received a hard copy and I lost it so I don't have the information on that. But is this sufficient in terms of the meaning of the Latin or do we need to get that document uploaded to complete the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it all about the explosive wound?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Looking at the record for this issue, I promised you many months ago to get you a translation of the Latin. CLSS came back with a translation that we frankly disagreed with the Defence on and we have not offered it. However, Mr. Ivetic has gone to a source that has described that and the way it was translated is, I think, fair, and I think we're willing to stand on the old translation and the testimony of this witness and he will, of course, be cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We leave it there for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we'll wait what later happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, now I wish to return to your expert work in relation to the Tomasica evidence of Dr. Clark, so I would ask that we now take a look at Exhibit D1447 marked for identification and that would be your report as to Dr. Clark and the Tomasica material. And ... I think you still have your copy in front of you as I don't have a clean copy in front of me. I'd like to turn to page 16 in e-court in the English and this will be page 22 of the original in Serbian. And we have... oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page in the Serbian. I appear to have miscounted. I see it's hard copy 22, it's in e-court, in the original Serbian. But we have here a list of sources that you used in your analysis and I wish to focus on two of these that are to be found on the next page in both language versions of the report. And I will wait for the e-court to catch up with us. And they are the second and third up from the bottom of the list and they deal with asanacija of the terrain or sanitisation as it has been translated. One of them deals with the identification of bodies in mass disasters, and the other talks about a kit, SNK69 for use in identifying bodies in mass disasters. Can you tell us how you came to prepare these two documents that are listed in the report as sources that you used. That is to say, how did you become -- how did you come to be requested to author these two documents?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: The second document, "Sanitisation of terrain in mass disasters," commissioned by Belgrade was a result of mass disasters in our city caused by either natural causes, earthquakes, floods or et cetera, or caused by war or terrorist action. The city of Belgrade did not have enough autopsy specialists who would deal with these bodies and the commander of civilian protection at the time, a certain Colonel Kovacevic who was in charge, knowing all this and bearing in mind the problems of sanitizing the terrain at the time when a plane from Zagreb fell when it was still the country of SFRY, asked that he be able to participate in drafting a document that would regulate sanitisation of terrain in the event of massive disasters. There were representatives of the army, the police, civilian structures involved in this work, and we produced a draft document that was first adopted by the Assembly -- Municipal Assembly of Belgrade and then proposed it to another municipalities to adopt for the same purpose. What did sanitisation of terrain mean? It meant primarily taking care of the terrain after an accident designating a place where bodies, human corpses and carcasses would be disposed of, a place where autopsies would be done. It designated who would be leaders of the teams and other experts necessary, what documentation produced should look like, how it would be presented, and various other related issues. After this draft document was made, we designated exact locations where bodies would be collected, who would be in charge of post-mortems, where we would look for assistance and from whom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question was how did you come to be requested to you author these two documents. Mr. Ivetic, it could be that witness is exactly telling what you wanted to ask him anyhow, but could we try to get focussed questions, focussed answers, such as this was triggered by this or that event or I was asked by the municipality, rather than to explain far beyond what was asked. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the first document is concerned, the Assembly of Belgrade asked me to do it. At that time, I was a well known expert in this area, and together with other experts, I was asked to do it. In the second case, it was the army who requested it because in the army there was a Department for the development of war sanitary equipment. They wanted a document about sanitisation in massive disaster there was already one set of procedures and rules, but they wanted it to be complemented and updated with an eye on how it is done in other countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you identified that it applies to war and terrorism et cetera. What was to be done in represent to explosives, weapons, and munitions found in -- in the asanacija or sanitisation process as it related to war?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: In some parts of the clothing of the soldiers we autopsied at the military medical academy, we found grenades, explosives, ammunition, bullets, and everything we found we handed over to the military police and they somehow stored it and disposed of it, and they gave it to the quartermaster service or whatever section in the army it is that deals with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And were there any instances when it was foreseen that full autopsies would not be able to be performed in mass disasters; if so what were those circumstances foreseen?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: A complete post-mortem implied opening bodily cavities according to the prescribed rules. A partial post-mortem implied an external description of the body while removing the clothing to see what personal items were there. A record would be made, and after that, the corpse would just be externally inspected to register injuries, the location of injuries, their appearance, their size, number, and whatever was possible to describe at the moment, and those were the characteristic body parts for identification. After that, the bodies were stored in designated locations, and then the people who did the exhumations could see the bodies again, if necessary, or remove parts of the body needed for DNA analysis and describe the injuries in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, focussing specifically on the asanacija that applies to war-time conditions or combat, what, according to the procedures was to be done for bodies found in the battle-field? Corpses found in the battle-field, what was to be done with them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what I said about partial autopsies, that also includes recording the body and describing it, including the clothing found on the body, external description of the parts that could be useful for identification, the dental status that is to be compared with dental records in health centres, and after that, the body, under a certain number, would be buried, and after the war, the bodies could be exhumed again for renewed post-mortem and collecting samples for further processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to turn to page 3 in both languages of D1447 MFI which we have in front of us, and I'd like to address with you the part A of your report which is: "Objections and unresolved issues regarding deviations from acceptable standards and procedures that follow from the contents of the report." And here in the first numbered paragraph -- oh, I have to wait for the B/C/S. Now I have to, I think, wait for the English. And you have written here under number one: "How is it possible for the chief ICTY pathologist in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia to offer his help with the exhumation and processing of bodies in Tomasica, receive his information about the grave-site in informal conversations, he does not state with whom, and say that his role was 'was an unofficial one' and that ICTY then requests him to draw up a report on autopsy findings?" Now, I want to break this down. First of all, the unofficial role of Dr. Clark in the investigations of Tomasica. Can you please tell us, from the perspective of the field of practice of forensic medicine, what is the standard role of a pathologist and how does it compare to this unofficial role of Clark?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that if somebody participates in work on a mass grave and the team is led by an investigating judge, then the leader of the post-mortem team is the one who assigns roles to every member of the post-mortem team. I cannot understand that somebody describes their role as unofficial, that they did not have any kind of mandate since this investigation was overseen by the prosecutor's office of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it would have been logical for the prosecutor to specify the role of Dr. Clark, in co-ordination with the Tribunal or something, I don't know. But, in any case it is completely impossible for somebody to come in from the street and say, I want to participate and help in the processing of this mass grave. From an expert point of view, it's unacceptable, and I, as an expert, I would never accept such a role in dealing with a mass grave. And then we can't find in the papers any detailed trace of Dr. Clark's role, but he proceeds to make a report on the case, although he was absent at the beginning of the exhumations and although he receives his information in what he calls informal conversations. Why didn't he conduct formal interviews with the leading people in the investigation who must have given him their approval to be there, otherwise he couldn't have been there? So why didn't he ask them also to give him access on all the resulting -- all the resulting information? That's why I made this remark about this work procedure and this way the report was written for such an important institution as the international Tribunal in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: From the perspective of your profession, what is the proper procedure for obtaining information via interviews when one is a forensic pathologist engaging in an investigation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: From the moment when the leaders of the investigation decide to engage you, the leader decides on your level of clearance. You can have contacts and hear other versions of events from other people. You can talk to other people involved in the work, processing the mass grave, but formally and legally, it is the investigating judge or the prosecutor who determine your role and you act accordingly, in keeping with their instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we could take a look at number 2 in your objections and unresolved issues, you say: "Why did Dr. Clark take notes and take photographs independently of Dr. Dzevad Durmisevic of Bihac and Professor Nermin Sarajlic from the Sarajevo University and can this be understood as mistrust of experts from Bosnia and Herzegovina." In your experience, where there are multiple forensic pathologists working together, what would be the commonly accepted procedure for this type of work, especially as to photography?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: It's very odd and very unprincipled to conduct a separate investigation within the framework of the investigation led by the official authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And for Dr. Clark to write a separate report without trying to harmonise what he wrote with Dr. Sarajlic and Dr. Durmisevic. It's the first time I hear of anything like that happening. Because if the doctors who were in charge got a man who is doing work off his own bat, I myself would never accept to work in such conditions. I would just tell the people in charge, I cannot go on. If this is the way you want it, you will do it without me. Because if he was officially engaged, then they had the obligation to harmonise their findings. Later on, when we get to the examples, we will see exactly what's wrong with it, and then the leader of the investigation should have tried to harmonise their findings. If he was unable to, then he would engage external experts and then we wouldn't have two different causes of death for one person, parts of the body that one doctor described and the other didn't, et cetera. It's also beyond my understanding that he, as a person who is producing a general report for the ICTY, makes his only photographs. On site, there must have been a scene-of-crimes team from the official authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina and he could have just pointed and asked them, Please make me photos of this or that body part. I can hardly imagine a forensic pathologist lowering himself to the role of a simple photographer. He is a renowned specialist with great experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You questioned here if Clark --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can I seek clarification. You say you can hardly imagine someone lowering -- apart from whether taking photographs is lowering for someone who has other capacities as well, but is there any suggestion that he did not take those photographs or -- I mean, do you not believe him? Or is it just that you are astonished by that cause of action which you, as a respected expert, would never have followed? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the main problem, in my view, is that a forensic pathologist's main focus should have been on analysing and qualifying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... witness, let me stop you there. Could I receive an answer to my question. Is it that you don't believe him that he took those photographs? Or is it that you would never have done that for professional reasons to do it as he says he did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe these people, but I find it hard to believe that they did this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I -- yes, but you, nevertheless, believe it. You do not -- I'm trying to understand your testimony, whether there's any suggestion that he's not telling the truth or that you think that he acted very unwise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I find it hard to believe that he acted in a way that is completely dissonant with his professional qualifications and that he did work that is not in his area of competence. I have no dilemma that he took his own photographs. That's not what I'm questioning; I believe that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You have answered my question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in the last part of this item number two, you question if Clark had mistrust for experts from Bosnia-Herzegovina. What is the reputation within the forensic medical community, historically as to the practice of forensic medicine in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say that forensic medicine in Bosnia-Herzegovina never had any prominent specialists in the former Yugoslavia. There was, for instance, Professor Vujicic [phoen] from the military medical academy who was practically the founder of forensic medicine in Bosnia-Herzegovina but in this specific case I'm not able to come up with any names of people who were particularly well-known in the area of forensic medicine and would have been generally accepted in the territory of former Yugoslavia. As for others, for instance, there was Dr. Curkic [phoen] in Doboj and Dr. Cirklas [phoen] in Tuzla, with whom I used to work. They are very good doctors. There is the late Dr. Dobraca, with whom I also worked. In Mostar he was a solid man. There was some others. I don't want to talk about them in this context. I don't know about Dr. Durmisevic and Dr. Sarajlic. I first came across their names through these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation to his arrival at the Tomasica investigations, and his role in the same, Dr. Clark testified in this trial and I would like to ask you about some of the things that he testified about. So I'd like to read to you his testimony from transcript page 36621, line 17 to 36623, line 16, and then I'll have some questions about that. So here comes the quotation: "Q. So it has to do with the procedure in the mortuary. You gave us an answer today as well, stating that you became involved in what is described here under number 3. You told us that the actions carried out in paragraphs 1 and 2 had already been carried out by other people. How long did this last, that is to say, what was described in paragraphs 1 and 2, opening bags, removing clothing for washing, and then cleaning the bodies themselves, all these things what the anthropologists did? "A. That process was already under way by the time I arrived at the mortuary. Really, from the time that the bodies started arriving from the site into the mortuary, local staff, some of them employed by ICMP, some of them probably not directly employed but they had started going through the bodies, removing the clothing to wash the bodies so that they could be examined by the anthropology team who would do an inventory of what bones and parts of the body were present, try and assess the sex of the individual from looking at the bones, and sometimes taking a sample at that stage, a bone sample or a tooth sample for DNA analysis. Once that was completed, the body would be sealed up again in the body bag, awaiting the pathologists to have a look at that in due course, examine the body in due course. We obviously could see the processes going on just in the general course of events, but we had no direct oversight over them. "Q. I do apologise, but you did not answer my question. For how long had the work already been done in terms of paragraphs 1 and 2 before you arrived and became involved in the Tomasica case? "A. I would imagine that probably one to two months. I don't know precisely the date, but it would be of that pat-- order. "Q. It would be a fair assessment to say that you had no knowledge whatsoever in terms of what had been done before you arrived there and before you started working on the Tomasica case. Would that be correct? "A. I was aware. I was aware that procedures had been carried out. I had not witnessed it directly myself. "Q. How was it that you were aware of the procedures that were applied? "A. When I did arrive, these procedures were still ongoing because there was so many bodies, so I was able to see the bodies being washed, and I was informed that a lot of other bodies had already been dealt with, so I could see -- I could see the process. It was still ongoing. And I could see -- similarly, I could see the process done by the anthropologists and the records that they kept and the details and the photography done, so I did at least see a substantial number of cases going through these procedures but only kind of -- from a distant, distant point of view. "Q. Did you try to intervene in relation to the procedures that were different from the ones that you had applied earlier on? "A. I made unofficial suggestions that this was a different way of doing things, but I realised I was very much the visitor. I had no official role there, that the exercise was now being run by the Bosnian Commission and that, well, I had -- I had little influence to change things." And now I'd like to ask you, professor, for your observations as an expert in this field about Dr. Clark's own description of his arrival on the scene and lack of involvement in the processes that were under way, that he himself said were being done in a different way.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot believe that he said this. If he said it and you say that he did, then it would be best if he were to withdraw his whole report which is now in front of us and that we would at least have a report on what the experts from Bosnia-Herzegovina did and what the investigation service of Bosnia-Herzegovina did. Firstly, there is no -- it's team-work led by the prosecutor in this specific case. The prosecutor co-ordinates all the activities. You as a pathologist come to the scene and together with other team members, you can see the bodies which are taken out of a mass grave. These are not war-time conditions and not investigations about -- let me not say anything disparaging. I believed that he was present during the post-mortem examination and that he communicated not only with pathologists and forensic experts but also anthropologists and prosecutors and everybody else because these are very complex issues. One cannot work like this and this statement shows that, in this specific case, Dr. Clark made a professional error and that after such a statement, this report is, in fact, I would say, such that it cannot be used in a trial proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we're at the time for the last break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are beyond that already. But after the long quote, I didn't want to disallow you to put a question to the witness. We'll take another break and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, I'd like to stay for a few more moments with the testimony we just went through of Dr. Clark from this trial. In relation to what he described, the cleaning of the remains that others did that he wasn't involved in, do you have any professional comment as to the manner in which it was said by Dr. Clark to have been carried out in relation to Tomasica?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: The forensic expert should be present from the beginning of the post-mortem examination. It should have been seen whether by the washing of the bodies some elements or evidence may be removed that might, for example, indicate a distance from which a projectile was fired because traces of gunpowder explosion may remain on the surface of the body and they may be partly removed but not completely. There may be gunpowder elements that are suffusing the soft tissues and may be detected by microscopic analysis. The projectile also has some dirt on its surface and by passing through clothes or the body, the dirt also leaves trace on the soft tissues or on the clothes so perhaps with this washing before the insight of the pathologist, such traces may have been destroyed. So it's difficult to understand how a doctor who examines the patients is not present during the exhumation where the body is exhumed when found and that he has no communication from the anthropologist who would indicate from his point of view whether certain segments of textile or body parts would need to be specifically analysed or focussed on, but rather come and see only a body that has been cleaned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I wish to also read a subsequent part of Dr. Clark's testimony, this time going from transcript page 36623, line 17, to 36625, line 2. And here begins the quotation: "Q. Could you please tell us now briefly how come you appeared at that location where the autopsies are carried out. You said beforehand that you were a volunteer and now you said that you were a visitor. Could somebody else have come there as a volunteer or visitor, whoever wished to do so? "A. Perhaps I've used the word 'visitor' loosely. I mean it to I was there with permission to be there but I was not in a position to change anything. The reason I was specifically involved was, it was suggested by Professor Sarajlic in Sarajevo that Dr. Durmisevic would probably welcome, very much welcome my assistance, given my past experience and my past interest in this work. So he was very welcoming and made arrangements for the Prosecutor to get permission for me to be there, so I wasn't just a casual visitor. I was there with specific permission because of expertise; but at the same time, I was conscious that I was there, I was taking my own -- making my own observations and that the two Bosnian pathologists were doing the official observations for their -- for their purposes for the Prosecutor. So -- and nobody else could have been there without permission. "Q. How come you became involved before permission was given? Was this at your own initiative? Did somebody ask you to do that? "A. Partly it was my initiative. I was in discussions with Professor Sarajlic about doing research on cases that both of us had seen -- had been involved in previously in Bosnia, particularly north of Bosnia, and he happened to mention that there was going to be work at the Tomasica site. It was quite a coincidence that it all happened at the same time, and he suggested that it would be good for me to be involved. I was able to be, and so it went on, and that -- that request was made into formal permission for me to be there. So it was a chance circumstance of time and availability. "Q. Could we say that it was actually your own initiative? "A. Yes, I didn't have to be there. The work would have gone on had I not been there, certainly. My involvement was also encouraged by both ICMP and ICTY. It just happened that, at that time, at that particular time, it was during a major conference actually here in The Hague involving ICMP and ICTY, so there was direct discussions during the conference, and they both encouraged and facilitated my involvement." Now, professor, from the standpoint of your profession, how do you regard Dr. Clark's definition of his role into the Tomasica investigative efforts as he described here in this part of his own testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: This part of his testimony is contrary to what he wrote in the report itself. Because in the report he writes that his role was unofficial, and now we are getting a different picture of his role. I think that it was really good that he came to the location to help the people who were working there and who did not have experience with processing mortal remains from a mass grave, but I also believe that his role, as described by him, including his arrival to the scene, is unacceptable. I would never agree to come and work in this manner, whoever invited me. I would have requested for the prosecutor of Bosnia-Herzegovina who was in charge of the investigation, ask for the approval of ICTY, not ICMP, because they are not important. They may request it, but the role and position of ICTY are important. So they should have been asked for approval of my presence because someone's responsibility was discussed before this Tribunal and perhaps also before a court in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And it was only after that, that it should have been asked for the prosecutor or investigating judge to issue an order and determine the role and mandate that I would have as part of the examination and processing of mortal remains of the bodies from the Tomasica mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can focus on the next item from your Tomasica report part A that is labelled as number 3 and that's at the -- whoops, at the bottom of the page in the Serbian and goes onto the next page in the Serbian. And it reads here: "If Dr. Clark co-operated with the forensic pathologists from Bosnia and Herzegovina '(usually) agreeing' with them, as he states in the report, then it follows that there were also some disagreements that are not mentioned in the report, and so the question arises as to whose finding and opinion the ICTY Trial Chamber accepts and why it has not ordered a harmonisation of various findings, or, if necessary, a new expert analysis?" And the first question I have for you, professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you put that question to the witness, could you first seek clarification as to what the "it" in the semi-last line refers to. Is it that the Trial Chamber or is it ... Who should have ordered a harmonisation of various findings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The person who was in charge of the investigation should have asked for harmonisation, in this specific case the prosecutor of Bosnia and Herzegovina or if the document was presented to ICTY, then the Prosecutor from ICTY. The Prosecutor was the one who presented the document to the Trial Chamber so he should have requested the harmonisation. If they didn't, then there is a possibility for the Trial Chamber to request that the findings be harmonised between the pathologists who have different opinions or then a new expert analysis that would then be presented to the Trial Chamber in the form of a document that would not include opposite opinions about the post-mortem examinations that were carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have another question before you ask the question. Professor, is it so that, indeed, the ICTY received two unharmonised reported or did they receive only one report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this specific case, I only had at my disposal one report, the report of Dr. Clark which was given to me for review. I did not see the reports of Bosnian pathologists or the prosecution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And as far as I have been informed, it is inexistent. But analysing the documents that were submitted to me, I compared autopsy reports drawn up by Dr. Clark and autopsy reports drawn up by Dr. Durmisevic and Dr. Sarajlic. In these autopsy reports, there are great differences about the situation, and I list them at the end of my report relating to Tomasica. This is why I thought and believed that it was necessary for Dr. Clark, Dr. Sarajlic and Dr. Durmisevic to sit down together and harmonise all the inconsistencies and then submit the results to ICTY. If Dr. Sarajlic requested that Dr. Clark should come because of Dr. Durmisevic's expertise, I can say that there are drastic differences between the findings of Professor Sarajlic and Dr. Clark. I found that when analysing their autopsy reports. I photocopied or rather printed out ten such autopsy reports drawn up by Dr. Durmisevic and Dr. Sarajlic and compared them with the findings, which I have here on the desk in front of me in a closed folder, so I compared them with the contents of Dr. Clark's report and I noticed the differences. And I believed that such an important Tribunal, founded by the most important global organisation, the United Nations cannot pass a judgement on the basis of such a document until the findings of the pathologists who were in charge of autopsies were harmonised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it your position that where two experts give two divergent opinions on an issue, it's open for either of Prosecution of this Court or of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the Tribunal to order them to harmonise their differences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that's not only my position. I think that's generally accepted rules, that applies in all courts, including the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can talk some more about this generally accepted process of harmonisation, how is it carried out in the ordinary course of forensic medical work, the harmonisation and the new expert analysis? How does this usually work out?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: After completing the post-mortem, if there are experts who were present and whose positions differ, then the leader of the investigation - that is to say, the investigative judge or the prosecutor - is notified, and he has the duty of recording these differences, trying to get the experts to agree. If that is impossible, then he commissioned a new forensic examination by different experts who have higher professional integrity and, thus, they obtain a new report, new findings, that can be accepted by the Trial Chamber. After providing such a report, the expert must defend their findings, be it on the instructions of the prosecutor or the Trial Chamber, but in any case, it all happens before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in your review of Dr. Clark's report and the other materials that you reviewed, was there evidence of any such process of harmonisation -- attempted harmonisation or engagement of a third independent expert considered or utilised?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. In the case file, there is no mention of any harmonisation of positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is there any explanation by Clark or the Bosnian pathologists of why it was not done in this case relating to Srebrenica -- relating to Tomasica?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: In the documents that I have, there is no explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then if we look at the next of your observations in paragraph 4, which is to be found on page 3 in English and page 4 in the Serbian original --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, would you allow me ask one question in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are pointing at the -- sometimes disagreement between the experts Dr. Clark and the BiH experts. In your report, you list, to start with, nine cases, where you say some of the cases in which inconsistency has been observed between the autopsy reports of Dr. Clark and the pathologist commissioned by the prosecutor of BiH and then you have one other example, which then follows, I think, in -- it's Annex C where you give cases of unacceptable conclusion and, as a matter of fact, you say "cases" but it is one case. Could you tell us, how many other cases you find similar substantial differences? So if these are examples, I would like to know how many in total you found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I made an analysis of the entire documentation, but I listed only these nine, in fact, ten examples that are typical, that involve differences in findings, and I thought -- I didn't record the exact number of discrepancies. That is to say, opposite findings, and I'm not able to tell you how many there are now. But I analysed all of them, and I singled out these as typical examples where we find completely opposite findings between Dr. Clark and the autopsy experts from Bosnia-Herzegovina because this is a sufficient number to show that differences exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I would be interested to know whether these are the ones that could be detected or whether there were far more on a total of how many? Do you remember how many in total you compared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think I compared about 100 cases. And among these hundred, not less than 20 involved differences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you would say the ten you listed, at least there is a double number which shows similar inconsistencies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you be so kind - we'll adjourn in a second - would you be so kind to identify those other tens you say -- those other ten you say are certainly there so that we can get a better impression. You said "at least another ten." But perhaps even if you find more, we'd be interested to assess the proper size of the inconsistencies you have found and not only by way of examples but -- have a full insight in how many there are. Would you be willing to spend part of your own free time to do that exercise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, Your Honour, I came here at your request, and I will do whatever you want me to do. My free time doesn't matter. So tomorrow ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's highly appreciated. Mr. Ivetic, we are at the time where we have to adjourn anyhow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But Judge Moloto -- yes, Mr. Ivetic, you had a question. I'll not -- we intervened, if you think it's important to put that question now right away, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No. It will take at least four minutes, I think, so it will put us well over the time to go to that new point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you -- and you can live with it? It doesn't disturb your --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I can live with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm at least glad to hear that. Mr. Stankovic, we'll adjourn for the day. I give you the same instructions as I did before for the breaks, that is, that you should not communicate, not speak, in whatever way, not communicate with whomever about your testimony, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 to continue to hear your evidence. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 19th of April, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 19th day of April, 2016, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.17 p.m.,
